**South-African Folk-Tales**

_by James A. Honeÿ_

## The Lost Message

There was once a chief who had a dispute with another chief about a river which was the boundary between them. They decided to submit the matter to the Great Chief, the white man's Governor, so they called a council.

When the council was over and they were all seated on the ground waiting for the decision, the Governor wrote a letter to the chief and gave it to one of his messengers.

"Take this to the chief," he said, "and return at once."

The messenger ran, and soon came to a river. On the opposite side he saw a beautiful girl, so he called out, "Please tell me where the chief is."

"He is at his kraal beyond the hill," she replied.

"Will you hold my letter while I wade across?" he asked. But she only laughed and said, "I cannot read."

So he waded across the river, and, when he got to the other side, he held out his hand for the letter. But, to his horror, it was gone. He looked everywhere, but could not find it. The girl had vanished, and the river had carried the letter away.

He was afraid to return to the Governor without the letter, so he went to the chief's kraal, thinking that he might be able to see the chief himself and deliver the message by word of mouth. But when he arrived at the kraal, the chief was not there, and the people refused to listen to him.

So he returned to the Governor and told him what had happened. The Governor was very angry, and said, "Because you have lost the letter, you shall be punished. You shall carry no more messages, but shall be a herdsman for the rest of your life."

And so it was. The man became a herdsman, and his children after him, because he lost the message entrusted to him.

## The Story of Lion and Little Jackal

Lion once met Little Jackal and said, "Let us hunt together, Little Jackal, and share what we kill."

"Very well, Father Lion," said Little Jackal, "but you must do the hunting, for I am small and weak."

So Lion hunted and killed a fine buck. Then he said, "Now we must divide it."

"Yes, Father Lion," said Little Jackal.

"I will take the meat, and you may have the bones," said Lion.

"Very well, Father Lion," said Little Jackal, meekly.

Lion took all the meat home to his wife and children. Little Jackal took the bones home to his wife and children, and they tried to eat them, but the bones were hard and dry.

So Jackal's wife said, "Why do you let Lion cheat you? Go back and demand your share of the meat."

"I dare not," said Little Jackal, "for Lion is strong and fierce."

"Then I will go myself," said his wife.

She dressed herself in her husband's skin and went to Lion's house. "Give me my share of the meat," she cried, in a deep voice.

Lion looked at her and was frightened, for he thought it was Little Jackal come back, and he gave her the best piece of meat.

Then she took the meat and ran home, and Little Jackal and his wife and children feasted that night.
